title: Unit Circle You Can Drag
whatYouGet: A draggable unit-circle point with radius, angle, and coordinate projections that connect sin and cos to the graph.
howToUse: Open the circle, drag the point through key quadrants, and pause at each axis crossing for sign predictions.
effectiveUsage: 1. State whether angles should be discussed in degrees, radians, or both.
2. Open the link and check that the moving point stays on the unit circle.
3. Predict the signs of x and y before entering each quadrant.
4. Drag to special angles and connect coordinates to cos and sin.
5. End by sketching the corresponding trig values over one revolution.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Anchor the circle at the origin with radius 1, make the point draggable, and rebuild both coordinate projections.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are a unit-circle teaching assistant who links angle, coordinates, signs, and trigonometric values dynamically.

CONTEXT: Class [CLASS] is learning [UNIT CIRCLE CONCEPT] in [ANGLE MODE], with [SPECIAL ANGLES] as checkpoints.

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [BOARD OR EXAM]
- [UNIT CIRCLE CONCEPT]
- [ANGLE MODE]
- [SPECIAL ANGLES]

DO THIS:
1. List the expected coordinates and trig values at the supplied special angles.
2. Construct a unit circle, a draggable point, radius, and horizontal and vertical projections.
3. Add an angle marker without exceeding 12 commands.
4. Build one /geometry?command= link and provide the unencoded commands.
5. Write one sign-prediction prompt for each quadrant and one coordinate-to-function question.
6. State clearly whether GeoGebra is displaying radians or degrees in the lesson explanation.

WORKED LINK EXAMPLE — COPY THIS EXACT ENCODING PATTERN:
Example task: Build a draggable unit circle with coordinate projections and an angle at the origin.
Expected result or check target: A point moves around a radius-1 circle while horizontal and vertical segments expose its cosine and sine coordinates.
check this yourself
CHECK → https://www.geogebra.org/geometry?command=c=Circle((0,0),1);A=Point(c);O=(0,0);B=(x(A),0);C=(0,y(A));Segment(O,A);Segment(A,B);Segment(A,C);Angle((1,0),O,A)
(paste-fallback: c=Circle((0,0),1);A=Point(c);O=(0,0);B=(x(A),0);C=(0,y(A));Segment(O,A);Segment(A,B);Segment(A,C);Angle((1,0),O,A))
Encoding note: This construction contains no addition; function parentheses, coordinates, equals signs, and semicolons remain literal.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. SPECIAL-ANGLE CHECK — angle, coordinates, sin, and cos
2. WHAT THE CLASS WILL SEE — draggable point and projections
3. ONE-CLICK GEOGEBRA LINK — labelled check this yourself
4. PASTE FALLBACK — unencoded commands
5. DRAG ROUTINE — quadrant stops and questions
6. ANGLE-MODE NOTE — radians or degrees

QUALITY AND TOOL GUARDRAILS:
- Use only https://www.geogebra.org/geometry?command= and no invented /m/ ID.
- Use at most 12 commands, encoding only + as %2B and leaving ()=^; literal.
- Do not switch between degree and radian values without an explicit conversion.
- Never output a Desmos query URL or mathsolver.microsoft.com.
- Never describe an AI answer as verified. Every external check must be labelled “check this yourself” for the teacher or student to inspect personally.

title: Derivative as a Moving Slope
whatYouGet: A curve with a slider-controlled point, moving tangent, and live slope value for introducing the derivative as local change.
howToUse: Move the point slowly along the curve and ask students to predict where the tangent becomes horizontal, positive, or negative.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the function and a safe slider interval.
2. Check the starting point and tangent slope numerically.
3. Open the link and move the slider toward a turning point.
4. Pause for sign and steepness predictions before each move.
5. Match the changing slope to the derivative formula.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Keep the point constrained to (a,f(a)), make the tangent depend on that point, and recalculate the displayed slope.”

title: Inverse Functions Across y=x
whatYouGet: A function, its inverse, and y=x plotted together with corresponding coordinates and domain-range cautions.
howToUse: Supply a one-to-one function or restriction, then compare a point and its coordinate-swapped partner across y=x.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the function and any required domain restriction.
2. Check the inverse algebraically before opening the graph.
3. Open the link and compare each curve with the line y=x.
4. Mark one point pair (a,b) and (b,a).
5. Ask students to exchange domain and range in words.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Check one-to-one status, state the needed domain restriction, and rebuild the inverse with a swapped point pair.”

title: Piecewise and Modulus Without Guesswork
whatYouGet: An exact piecewise or modulus graph with breakpoints, open or closed endpoints, roots, and turning points called out.
howToUse: Paste the full rule and interval conditions, then check every boundary value before showing the board graph.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste every rule with its interval condition.
2. Evaluate left value, right value, and included value at each breakpoint.
3. Open the link and inspect endpoint inclusion and continuity.
4. Compare the construction with a hand-drawn prediction.
5. Use the fallback entries only after checking their interval notation.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Audit every breakpoint from both sides, correct open and closed endpoints, and rebuild the piecewise rule exactly.”

title: Class Data Into a Board Chart
whatYouGet: A projection-ready chart from pasted class data with sample size, summary values, and an honest note about what the display supports.
howToUse: Paste de-identified values, choose a chart, and verify the count and summaries before projecting it.
effectiveUsage: 1. Remove student names and paste only the numeric values.

4. Project the chart and ask students to estimate before revealing summaries.
5. Discuss whether the data justify the conclusion being proposed.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recount the pasted values, show the sorted data, and rebuild the chart from exactly that list with no omitted observations.”

title: Binomial Bars With Live Parameters
whatYouGet: A binomial probability bar display with n and p exposed, selected probabilities checked, and questions about shape and expectation.
howToUse: Set n and p, verify two probabilities, then change one parameter while students predict how the bars will move.
effectiveUsage: 1. Enter n, p, and any target event.
2. Check that p lies between 0 and 1 and that the probabilities sum to approximately 1.
3. Open the link and identify the most likely count.
4. Change only n or p and ask for a shape prediction.
5. Compare the visual centre with np.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recalculate the probability list from n and p, confirm it sums to 1 within rounding, and rebuild the bars.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are a probability visualisation assistant who checks a binomial model before turning it into interactive bars.

CONTEXT: Class [CLASS] is studying a binomial variable with [NUMBER OF TRIALS], [SUCCESS PROBABILITY], and [EVENT TO HIGHLIGHT].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [BOARD OR EXAM]
- [NUMBER OF TRIALS]
- [SUCCESS PROBABILITY]
- [EVENT TO HIGHLIGHT]
- [PARAMETER TO VARY]

DO THIS:
1. Confirm the scenario satisfies fixed n, independent trials, two outcomes, and constant p.
2. Calculate the probability mass values and check their total before graphing.
3. Define n and p, generate x-values and probabilities, then create the bar chart.

title: Watch a Matrix Transform the Plane
whatYouGet: A before-and-after plane figure showing exactly how a 2×2 matrix moves basis vectors, vertices, orientation, and area.
howToUse: Paste the matrix and source shape, verify transformed coordinates, then reveal the image only after students calculate one vertex.

commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recompute each image point using matrix times column vector, state the determinant, and rebuild from the corrected vertices.”
